title: Installing SQL tools: Windows, macOS, and Linux

questions.prompt: Which statement gives the core rule for “Installing SQL tools: Windows, macOS, and Linux”?
options: Start with a small, readable SELECT query; connect it to an application only after you understand its result.
Check SQLite with sqlite3 --version; sqlite3 school.db opens a local database file.
SQLite often runs inside the application; MySQL and PostgreSQL commonly run as separate server processes.
The query returns Ada and 42 in two columns.
questions.answer: Check SQLite with sqlite3 --version; sqlite3 school.db opens a local database file.
questions.explanation:
Check SQLite with sqlite3 --version; sqlite3 school.db opens a local database file.
Why: A SQL setup has two parts: a database engine and a tool for writing queries and viewing results. SQLite is a friendly start because it runs in one file without a server; DB Browser for SQLite adds a graphical interface. On Windows, download the command-line tools from SQLite's official download page and add their folder to PATH. On macOS, Homebrew can install them with `brew install sqlite`; on Debian/Ubuntu use `sudo apt install sqlite3`. For other Linux distributions, use their official package manager. PostgreSQL provides official installers and OS-specific instructions for all three systems. DB Browser packages are also available for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Verify with `sqlite3 --version`, open a practice file with `sqlite3 school.db`, and exit with `.quit`.
